newsitem.title: USA: Ireland's Bruton sees Britain, Denmark joining EMU.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Bruton sees Britain, Denmark joining EMU.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Wednesday that he believes Britain and Denmark would eventually join the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), even if the two countries opted out of an initial deadline set for January 1, 1999.

Bruton predicted that EMU, which calls for creation of a single European currency, would end economic instability and uncertainty caused by exchange rate fluctuation within the European Union and lower interest rates in some countries.
Britain and Denmark can avoid joining EMU under terms of the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.
"We cannot at this stage say if they will join in the enterprise from the beginning," Bruton said in remarks prepared for a speech to an audience of business leaders, academics and diplomats.
"Even if they do not join at the start, I am convinced that economic logic will lead them to do so after a little time."
The Irish prime minister went on to blame the British press for U.S. skepticism over EMU's likely success.
"This is not a good source on the subject," Bruton said of the British press.
"Take it from me: the single European currency will happen and will happen on time. There is an unstoppable political will and momentum behind it," he said.
Ireland held the rotating European presidency until last December.

Bruton predicted that the new European currency, the euro, would come to rival the U.S. dollar over time as a reserve currency, noting a current imbalance between the economic importance of the dollar and the size of U.S. exports.

"Today, the dollar still accounts for 60 percent of the exchange reserves of all central banks; it is involved in 50 percent of the world's commercial transactions and 80 percent of exchange transactions," he said.
"At the same time, the United States accounts for only 18 percent of world exports. There is clearly an imbalance here."
Bruton's remarks were prepared for an address at the Atlanta-based Southern Centre for International Studies.
